lab.title: Create a security baseline for a fictional organization
lab.brief: You have joined the security team of Northstar Library, a fictional service with a public website, staff laptops, a member database, and a small cloud account. Use only the supplied scenario facts. No live systems are involved.
steps: List the business services, information assets, owners, and users described in the scenario.
For each asset, state the confidentiality, integrity, and availability needs and explain the business impact of a failure.
Create three risk statements using the format: threat + weakness + affected asset + consequence.
Map at least one preventive, detective, and recovery control to each high-priority risk.
Draft a one-page authorization and scope note for a hypothetical assessment, including exclusions, contacts, time window, and stop conditions.
Present a short briefing that separates confirmed facts, assumptions, and unanswered questions.
evidence: Control map and written scope note

sections.heading: Think in assets and outcomes
body: Start by asking what the organization is trying to protect and why it matters. An asset can be information, a service, a device, an identity, a supplier relationship, or the ability to operate. Assign an owner so decisions have a responsible person.

Describe impact in ordinary business terms: interrupted service, altered records, exposed personal information, financial loss, safety concerns, or loss of trust. Avoid treating a tool alert as the risk itself.

sections.heading: Use a consistent risk model
body: A useful risk statement connects a threat, a weakness or exposure, an asset, and a plausible consequence. Record likelihood, impact, existing controls, uncertainty, and the person responsible for treatment.
Risk ratings are prioritization aids, not scientific measurements. Keep the scale simple, define it, and explain why a rating was chosen. Revisit it when the environment or evidence changes.

sections.heading: Choose layered controls
body: Preventive controls reduce the chance of an event; detective controls improve the chance of noticing it; responsive controls limit its effects; recovery controls restore a trustworthy service. One control rarely covers every failure mode.
Prefer controls that can be verified. A backup policy is not enough: restoration must be tested. A security policy is not enough: people need ownership, training, and a way to report exceptions.

sections.heading: Work professionally
body: Written authorization must identify the owner, approved assets, allowed activities, time window, data rules, contacts, and stop conditions. If the scope is unclear or the environment differs from the brief, pause and ask the owner.
Keep evidence minimal, protect it, record how it was obtained, and share it only with authorized recipients. Report limitations and uncertainty instead of presenting assumptions as facts.

assessment.q: A service is available, but its records have been changed without approval. Which security property is primarily affected?
assessment.why: Integrity concerns whether information remains accurate and is changed only through authorized processes.

assessment.q: A practical assessment brief does not identify which systems are in scope. What is the professional next step?
opts: Test only the systems that look interesting
Pause and obtain written scope from the owner
assessment.why: Written authorization and clear scope are prerequisites. Good intentions do not replace permission.

lab.title: Review and harden a fictional Linux workstation
lab.brief: A supplied inventory and configuration snapshot describe a fictional staff workstation. You will assess the configuration on paper and in a prepared local training image if one is provided. Do not change your everyday device or a shared computer.
steps: Read the system inventory and identify the operating-system version, owner, business purpose, and support status.
Review the supplied user and group table; flag shared accounts and administrator access without an owner or reason.
Compare the file-permission examples with the stated job tasks and identify where access is broader than necessary.
Review the baseline checklist for updates, disk encryption, screen lock, firewall, logging, and backup status.
Choose two low-risk hardening changes, record the expected effect, rollback approach, and verification evidence.
Write a short change record with before/after state, owner, test result, and any accepted exception.
evidence: Two change records with verification and rollback notes

sections.heading: Understand the host before changing it
body: Record operating-system edition, patch level, hardware role, owner, installed services, and the data it handles. An unsupported host should be treated as a lifecycle risk, not merely an update reminder.
Identify which services are required for the business task. A secure baseline starts from a known purpose and removes unnecessary exposure without breaking supported work.

sections.heading: Apply least privilege
body: Use named user accounts and groups that map to real responsibilities. Separate day-to-day work from administration, and give service accounts only the permissions their process requires.
For each file or directory, check owner, group, and access needs. Avoid broad write permissions as a quick fix. Record the reason for exceptions and assign an owner and review date.

sections.heading: Protect and observe endpoints
body: Keep supported operating systems and applications updated through a controlled process. Use disk encryption, automatic screen locking, host firewall policy, and endpoint protection appropriate to the device.
Collect useful security events while limiting sensitive data in logs. Verify that time is synchronized and that important events can be delivered to the central monitoring system.

sections.heading: Make changes safely
body: Use a change record: purpose, scope, owner, risk, planned action, test, rollback, and result. Start with one change at a time so the cause of an unexpected outcome is clear.
Verify both security and usability after a change. Confirm that approved users can still perform their work, that logs are generated, and that the host remains recoverable.

assessment.q: A team proposes making a shared application directory writable by every local user to fix a permissions error. What is the best response?
opts: Apply it because the app needs to write files
Identify the exact process and required path, then grant the narrowest access
assessment.why: Least privilege means granting only the access required by the specific service and operation.

assessment.q: A workstation is missing several security updates. What evidence best demonstrates that remediation is complete?
opts: An email saying the update was started
A current patch inventory and a successful verification/restart record
A note that the device is used rarely
assessment.why: The result must be verified in the system inventory, including the resulting patch level and any required restart.

guide.title: Network security and traffic interpretation guide

sections.heading: Follow the complete path
body: A user-facing request may involve local DNS, a recursive resolver, routing, a transport connection, TLS negotiation, a proxy, and an application service. Record each stage instead of treating the hostname as the whole connection.
Use the approved diagram and inventory to identify the expected source, destination, purpose, and owner. A port or protocol alone does not establish that a service is safe or unsafe.

sections.heading: Interpret evidence carefully
body: A packet summary can reveal timing, endpoints, protocol metadata, and some unencrypted content. TLS normally protects application payloads, but some connection metadata may still be visible to observers on the path.
A missing event can mean collection was unavailable, delayed, filtered, or incomplete. Record the data source and capture boundary before drawing conclusions.

sections.heading: Design network boundaries
body: Separate user devices, administrative access, public services, application components, and sensitive data stores according to business purpose. Permit only documented flows that have an owner and reason.
Review rules after changes and periodically. Remove expired exceptions, log important allowed and denied events, and test that legitimate service paths still work.

sections.heading: Make recommendations actionable
body: For every recommendation, name the affected zone, owner, business purpose, expected benefit, operational impact, and validation method. Prefer small, testable changes with a rollback plan.
Do not infer compromise from a single unfamiliar address. Correlate network observations with endpoint, identity, application, and change records.

assessment.q: A packet summary shows a TLS connection to a service. What can you safely conclude from that fact alone?
opts: The server is free of vulnerabilities
A TLS connection was negotiated, but service trust and security need further evidence
assessment.why: TLS helps protect a connection, but does not prove that the application is safe or that a user was authorized.

assessment.q: A network rule allows every user segment to reach a sensitive database. What is the best first design improvement?
opts: Document the reason and keep it forever
Restrict access to the specific application/service path and approved roles
Move the database to a public subnet
assessment.why: Network segmentation should allow only necessary, owned, and documented flows.

lab.title: Prioritize a fictional vulnerability backlog
lab.brief: Review a synthetic asset register and a set of fictional vulnerability advisories. No scanning or interaction with real systems is required.
steps: Normalize the asset list by owner, purpose, environment, exposure, and data sensitivity.
For each advisory, identify affected versions, preconditions, published fix, and uncertainty.
Rank the work using asset criticality, exposure, severity, and compensating controls—not severity alone.
Assign a remediation owner and target date; record a temporary exception only when justified.
Define a safe validation plan based on the vendor fix and approved change process.
Prepare a dashboard summary for a security lead, including overdue and blocked items.

sections.heading: Build an accurate inventory
body: Capture a stable asset identifier, type, owner, business service, environment, location, data classification, and lifecycle state. Reconcile inventories from endpoint, identity, cloud, and procurement sources.
An asset without an owner is difficult to protect. Assign an accountable owner and define how changes, exceptions, and retirement are reflected in the register.

sections.heading: Read advisories in context
body: Record the affected product and version, required configuration, exposure conditions, vendor fix, and workaround. Distinguish a vulnerability identifier from proof that a particular asset is affected.
Do not treat a severity score as a complete priority decision. An internet-facing system holding sensitive records may need faster action than a more severe issue on an isolated disposable test host.

sections.heading: Prioritize and remediate
body: Combine technical severity with asset value, network exposure, exploitability evidence, business impact, and existing controls. State the reason for each priority so another reviewer can reproduce the decision.
Assign an owner, deadline, validation method, and rollback plan. Temporary mitigations need an expiry date and a plan to remove the underlying weakness.

sections.heading: Prove closure
body: Verify the installed version or configuration after change and preserve the change record. If validation cannot be performed, state that limitation rather than closing the issue based on an email or ticket status.
Track exceptions, recurring weaknesses, overdue items, and the age of the backlog. Use trends to improve patch processes and asset ownership, not only to report a raw count.

assessment.q: A critical advisory affects a public-facing service that stores customer records. Which factor should most strongly influence remediation priority?
opts: Asset importance, exposure, affected version, and available mitigation
Whether the ticket title is short
assessment.why: Prioritization combines technical information with asset criticality, exposure, and practical mitigations.

assessment.q: A ticket is marked fixed, but no one verified the running version. What is the correct status?
opts: Closed because the ticket says so
assessment.why: Closure requires evidence that the intended version or configuration is actually present.

lab.title: Review a sample identity and access matrix
lab.brief: Use a fictional organization, role table, and access records. The task is to improve the design and verify business permissions, not to access a real account.
steps: List people, service identities, roles, data classes, and approval owners in the supplied scenario.
Compare each granted permission with the job task and flag shared, dormant, orphaned, or excessive access.
Design a role matrix with deny-by-default behavior and separate approval for privileged changes.
Review sample cases for account creation, role change, departure, expired session, and denied object access.
Specify MFA and session requirements for standard and privileged roles.
Produce an access-review record with owner, decision, evidence, and expiry date for exceptions.

sections.heading: Manage the full identity lifecycle
body: Create a unique identity for each person or service and connect it to an accountable owner. Define approval, provisioning, change, suspension, and removal steps for joiners, movers, and leavers.
Use periodic reconciliation to find accounts that no longer match the HR, contractor, or service inventory. Dormant accounts and orphaned service identities need a documented owner and decision.

sections.heading: Strengthen authentication
body: Use MFA according to risk, especially for administration, remote access, and sensitive data. Phishing-resistant factors are preferable where the platform supports them and the risk justifies them.
Protect recovery methods as carefully as primary authentication. A secure login can be undermined by weak account recovery, shared inboxes, or unreviewed backup factors.

sections.heading: Authorize every action
body: Authentication establishes an identity; authorization decides what that identity may do. Check permissions on the server for each protected action and object, not only when drawing the interface.
Use roles tied to job responsibilities, deny by default, and separate high-impact duties where practical. Test both allowed and denied cases, including changed roles and expired sessions.

sections.heading: Govern privileged and machine access
body: Give privileged accounts separate day-to-day identities, record approvals, and review their use. Service identities need an owner, limited purpose, stored secrets, rotation rules, and an exit plan.

Protect session identifiers with secure cookie settings over HTTPS, rotate sessions after authentication or privilege changes, and invalidate them on sign-out. Do not store long-lived credentials in browser storage.

assessment.q: A user can view their own invoice but can also change the record identifier in a request and view another customer record. Which control failed?
assessment.why: The server must verify permission for the specific record on every protected request.

assessment.q: A contractor leaves the organization. What should happen to their access?
opts: Keep it in case they return
Disable the identity and revoke active sessions/tokens according to policy
Wait for the next annual review
assessment.why: The leaver process should promptly disable access and revoke active credentials or sessions.

lab.title: Verify sample files and inspect a training certificate
lab.brief: Use non-sensitive sample files and a certificate prepared for the course. The exercise tests selection of controls and interpretation of evidence; it does not ask learners to create or deploy trust infrastructure.
steps: Record a checksum for each supplied sample file and note the algorithm and file name.
Compare the checksum of an unchanged copy with one where a harmless byte has been changed; explain the integrity signal.
Classify each example as encoding, hashing, encryption, authentication, or signature.
Read the sample certificate subject, issuer, validity period, key usage, and chain status.
Complete a key inventory with purpose, owner, location category, rotation, revocation, and recovery requirements.
Write a short note explaining what the evidence proves and what it does not prove.

sections.heading: Choose the security property
body: Hashing produces a fixed-length digest useful for detecting changes; encryption protects confidentiality; a message authentication code helps verify integrity and possession of a shared secret; a digital signature supports integrity and origin verification.
Encoding changes representation, not secrecy. A checksum does not prove who created a file, and a valid signature does not automatically make the signed content safe.

sections.heading: Protect password verifiers
body: Store passwords with a dedicated password-hashing function designed to be slow and configurable. Use a unique salt per password and review work parameters as computing capabilities change.
Never store plaintext passwords or use a fast general-purpose hash as a password verifier. Keep any additional server-side secret separate and protect access to the credential store.

sections.heading: Manage keys and certificates
body: Assign an owner and documented purpose to every key. Define secure generation, storage, access, rotation, backup, revocation, and destruction processes before a key is used.

Certificate review includes subject name, issuer, validity, key usage, and the chain to a trust anchor configured for the environment. A valid certificate does not prove that an application is trustworthy.

sections.heading: Record evidence and limits
body: Record the algorithm, parameters, tool, input file, timestamp, and outcome. Preserve the original evidence so another person can reproduce the check.
State the scope of each conclusion. A matching hash supports byte-for-byte consistency; it does not establish authorship, business correctness, or absence of malware.

assessment.q: What does a matching checksum of two files support?
opts: Evidence that the byte sequences match under the chosen algorithm
Proof that the file is safe to open
Proof that the file is confidential
assessment.why: A matching digest supports integrity comparison for the supplied bytes, not authorship or safety.

assessment.q: Which statement best describes a cryptographic hash used for file-integrity checking?
opts: It hides the file contents so they can be recovered later
It produces a fixed-length digest that changes when the input changes
It proves who created the file
It replaces the need to protect the original file
assessment.why: A hash digest is useful for detecting change when compared with a trusted reference. It does not encrypt data or establish who produced it.

lab.title: Review a deliberately vulnerable local training application
lab.brief: Use the provided source excerpts and test cases for a fictional application in a local training environment. Do not test public websites or services.
steps: Record the application version, roles, synthetic records, and allowed test cases.
Trace one request from the browser to the server-side handler and identify trust boundaries.
Review whether the server checks the current user and requested record on every protected operation.
Inspect validation, parameterized data access, output handling, cookies, error messages, and log content.
For each finding, state impact, evidence, root cause, recommended fix, and a safe regression test.
Re-run the supplied positive and negative cases and record any untested area.

sections.heading: Start with architecture
body: Identify users, roles, entry points, APIs, data stores, external services, and trust boundaries. Trace how sensitive data enters, moves through, and leaves the application.
Record the repository revision, test environment, allowed test accounts, and supplied cases. Review the design before focusing on individual fields or endpoints.

sections.heading: Enforce server-side authorization
body: The browser is not a security boundary. A hidden button or unlinked page does not prevent a user from sending a request directly. The server must check the current identity and permission for the specific object and action.
Use deny-by-default rules and test both permitted and denied access for multiple synthetic roles. Include changed roles, missing sessions, and attempts to access another sample user record.

sections.heading: Handle input, output, and secrets
body: Validate on the server against expected types, lengths, ranges, and business rules. Use parameterized data access and context-aware output encoding rather than ad hoc string filtering.
Keep secrets out of source control, browser code, URLs, and logs. Use generic user-facing errors and access-controlled diagnostics that avoid passwords, tokens, and unnecessary personal data.

sections.heading: Verify fixes and report
body: A finding should state the affected component, preconditions, observed behavior, impact, evidence, confidence, and recommended remediation. Separate confirmed behavior from possible consequences.
Add a regression test tied to the root cause, run the approved test suite, and record limitations. A small training result is not proof that an entire production system is secure.

assessment.q: A page hides an administrative button, but the server does not check permissions on the corresponding API request. Is access control correctly implemented?
opts: No, the server must authorize each protected action and object
Yes, if the URL is not linked
assessment.why: Authorization must be enforced on the server for each protected request; UI hiding is not a security control.

assessment.q: A user changes a record identifier in an API request. Which design must prevent access to another customer’s record?
opts: A hidden button in the interface
A server-side authorization check for that specific record
assessment.why: The server must check the authenticated identity against the requested object on every protected operation.

lab.title: Review a fictional software delivery pipeline
lab.brief: Review a supplied CI pipeline summary, dependency inventory, and release checklist. All examples are static and synthetic; there is no live repository or service to attack.
steps: Map the pipeline stages from code review through artifact creation, test, approval, and deployment.
Mark where secrets, signing material, deployment identities, and production approvals are used.
Review the supplied dependency list and advisory summaries; identify unsupported or affected components.
Propose a small set of checks that provide useful feedback without creating unowned alert noise.

sections.heading: Shift security into design
body: Security requirements should be specific enough to test: who may access a feature, what data is stored, how long it is retained, and what happens when dependencies fail. Include abuse cases and privacy needs during design.
Use threat modeling to find trust boundaries and risky flows before implementation. Revisit the model when architecture, data, or exposure changes materially.

sections.heading: Review code and dependencies
body: Code review should examine authorization, validation, data access, error handling, logging, and secret handling. A clean style review does not replace a security review.
Maintain a component inventory with version, source, support status, and owner. Review advisories in context and define how urgent updates are tested and released.

sections.heading: Protect build and release systems
body: Limit who can change pipeline definitions, approve production releases, and access deployment identities. Separate ordinary developer credentials from release credentials.
Keep secrets out of source code and build logs. Protect build artifacts, track their source revision, and use integrity mechanisms appropriate to the release process.

sections.heading: Make security checks actionable
body: Choose automated checks that match the technology and risk. Give every finding a route to an owner, a useful explanation, and a repeatable way to verify a fix.
Use risk-based thresholds and a time-bound exception process. Track false positives, escaped issues, and time to remediation so the pipeline improves rather than becoming a box-ticking exercise.

assessment.q: A pipeline detects a dependency issue. What makes the finding operationally useful?
opts: A red status with no details
Affected component and version, context, owner, remediation path, and verification
A long list of unrelated warnings
assessment.why: Security checks need context, ownership, remediation guidance, and a way to verify closure.

assessment.q: A build pipeline reports a high-risk dependency issue. What makes the response process complete?
opts: Assigning an owner, assessing exposure, selecting a fix, and verifying the released artifact
assessment.why: A useful pipeline finding has context, ownership, remediation, and evidence that the corrected artifact was released.

lessons.outcome: Identify management-plane protections and configuration ownership.

lessons.title: Resilience and recovery
lessons.outcome: Review redundancy, configuration backups, and recovery testing.

lessons.title: Architecture review mission
lessons.outcome: Present a prioritized plan with operational trade-offs and validation.

lab.title: Review a fictional enterprise network design
lab.brief: Use a supplied architecture diagram, firewall-rule table, and remote-access policy. This is a documentation review; do not connect to or probe any network.
steps: Identify public, user, server, administration, backup, and sensitive-data zones.
Map each documented business flow to a source, destination, purpose, owner, and protocol family.
Flag broad, ownerless, duplicate, or expired firewall rules in the supplied table.
Review remote-access requirements for MFA, managed devices, approval, logging, and session expiry.
Assess how network configuration is backed up, reviewed, and restored after an approved change.
Deliver a revised zone diagram and a prioritized remediation plan with validation criteria.

sections.heading: Design zones around purpose
body: Separate public-facing components, user devices, application tiers, sensitive data, administration, and backup services. The exact zones should reflect the business architecture and trust boundaries rather than a generic diagram.
Document permitted flows with a source, destination, service purpose, owner, and review date. A rule without a business owner is a candidate for review, not an assumed requirement.

sections.heading: Govern firewall policy
body: Use change control for firewall rules. Review broad address ranges, duplicate rules, temporary exceptions, and rules that no longer match an application inventory.
Prefer narrow, documented access paths. Log important administrative and denied events, but avoid collecting unnecessary content or personal data.

sections.heading: Protect remote administration
body: Require strong authentication and managed devices for administrative access. Separate administrative paths from ordinary user access and limit who may reach management interfaces.

Use individual accounts, time-bounded approvals where appropriate, session logging, and prompt revocation when a role changes. Do not expose management interfaces to the public internet as a convenience.

sections.heading: Plan for recovery
body: Keep protected configuration backups and record the version associated with each approved change. Test restoration using a planned maintenance exercise.
Resilience includes people and procedures: identify a service owner, an escalation contact, a recovery objective, and the evidence required to declare a service trustworthy again.

assessment.q: A firewall rule has no owner, no documented business purpose, and has remained for years. What is the best action?
opts: Keep it because old rules are probably needed
Review it with the service owner and remove or narrow it through change control if no longer justified
Copy it to every network zone
assessment.why: Rules need documented purpose and ownership. Changes should be reviewed and validated through change control.

assessment.q: A network review finds broad access between user devices and a sensitive service. What is the strongest design principle to apply?
opts: Allow all internal traffic by default
Permit only documented flows required by the service, with an owner and review date
assessment.why: Segmentation should reflect business flows and least privilege; rules need a reason, owner, and review.

en.title: Cloud, containers & infrastructure security
overview: Understand shared responsibility and cloud identity, network, storage, and logging controls.
Review configuration-as-code and change histories for security-relevant drift.
Understand container image, runtime, secret, and orchestration security concepts.
Create a practical cloud hardening and recovery checklist.

lessons.title: Shared responsibility and cloud identity
lessons.outcome: Separate provider controls from customer configuration and access decisions.

lessons.title: Cloud network and storage controls
lessons.outcome: Review exposure, encryption, backup, and data-owner requirements.

lessons.title: Infrastructure as code review

lessons.title: Container image and runtime hygiene
lessons.outcome: Understand base images, patching, privileges, and runtime boundaries.

lessons.title: Orchestration and secret management
lessons.outcome: Review workload identity, namespace boundaries, and secret ownership.

lessons.title: Cloud incident readiness
lessons.outcome: Define logs, backup ownership, evidence sources, and recovery actions.

lab.title: Audit a synthetic cloud and container environment
lab.brief: Review a fictional cloud configuration export, storage policy, identity-role map, and container inventory. No cloud account or live cluster is required.
steps: Identify which controls belong to the provider and which remain the customer responsibility.
Review the sample identity-role map for excessive permissions and ownerless service identities.
Inspect the storage and network configuration summary for unintended public exposure and missing recovery evidence.
Compare image and workload inventory with the stated patch, provenance, and runtime policies.
Review the infrastructure-as-code change summary and identify security-impacting drift or unreviewed changes.
Create a prioritized hardening plan with control owner, evidence, and recovery validation.

sections.heading: Understand shared responsibility
body: The provider secures facilities and managed service layers according to the service model. The customer remains responsible for choices such as identities, data, configuration, workload code, and access policy.
Write down the service model and map each required control to an owner. Avoid assuming that a managed service automatically makes data public/private, encrypted, backed up, or correctly permissioned.

sections.heading: Protect cloud identities and data
body: Use individual identities, role-based permissions, MFA for privileged operations, and scoped service identities. Review unused roles and credentials as part of the normal lifecycle.
Classify data and define location, retention, encryption, backup, and deletion requirements. Check access policy and recovery evidence rather than relying only on a configuration label.

sections.heading: Harden containers and orchestration
body: Use maintained base images, track image provenance, remove unnecessary packages, and scan images through an approved build process. Run workloads with the minimum privileges their purpose requires.
Separate workloads with appropriate identity and namespace boundaries. Protect orchestration control planes, restrict secret access, and keep runtime events available for investigation.

sections.heading: Review infrastructure changes
body: Treat infrastructure definitions as code: review changes, use version history, assign owners, and validate the resulting environment. Detect drift between the approved definition and deployed state.
Plan for cloud-region, identity, storage, and key-service failures. Backups should be protected from the same administrative path as production and recovery should be tested.

assessment.q: In a managed cloud service, who remains responsible for customer identity permissions and data classification?
opts: The customer, under the shared-responsibility model
assessment.why: The exact division varies by service model, but customers remain responsible for their identities, data, and configuration choices.

assessment.q: A cloud workload needs to access one storage service. Which identity pattern is generally preferable to a long-lived embedded key?
opts: A scoped workload identity or role with limited permissions
A key copied into source control
assessment.why: Workload identities and scoped roles reduce secret sprawl and make permissions easier to review and revoke.

en.title: Logging, SIEM & detection engineering
overview: Understand endpoint, identity, network, application, and cloud telemetry sources.
Normalize event fields and correlate timestamps while preserving original evidence.
Build detection logic with a purpose, data source, threshold rationale, and false-positive analysis.
Triage alerts using context, severity, confidence, and business impact.

lessons.title: Telemetry sources and event schemas
lessons.outcome: Select sources needed to answer a defined security question.

lessons.title: Time, identity, and normalization
lessons.outcome: Normalize timestamps and fields without losing source context.

lessons.title: Correlation and baselines
lessons.outcome: Connect related events and distinguish expected operational activity.

lessons.title: Detection logic and alert quality
lessons.outcome: Define event source, grouping, time window, threshold, and exceptions.

lessons.title: Triage, severity, and escalation
lessons.outcome: Write a concise evidence-based triage decision.

lessons.title: Detection tuning and metrics
lessons.outcome: Improve signal quality and measure coverage, false positives, and response time.

lab.title: Investigate a synthetic alert set
lab.brief: Use synthetic authentication, endpoint, and application events with fictional users and reserved addresses. The exercise is a defensive analysis of supplied logs.
steps: Document each event source, collection point, timestamp type, and known field gaps.
Normalize event time while preserving the original timestamp and source identifier.
Group related events by host, user, application, and source; distinguish expected automation from unusual sequences.
Draft a detection hypothesis with a named behavior, time window, grouping key, and threshold rationale.
Triage the supplied alert: severity, confidence, affected asset, evidence, and next owner.
Propose one tuning change and define how you will measure whether it improves signal quality.

sections.heading: Know your telemetry
body: Useful telemetry includes identity events, endpoint state, application audit records, network metadata, cloud control-plane events, and changes to security controls. Select sources based on the questions the team must answer.
Document collection coverage, retention, access controls, parsing version, time synchronization, and known gaps. A dashboard cannot compensate for missing or unreliable source data.

sections.heading: Build a defensible timeline
body: Preserve original events and normalize them for correlation. Record event time separately from collection time where both are available, and note timezone assumptions.
Correlate by stable identifiers such as host, account, request, and session. Avoid joining records solely because they are close in time; explain why events are believed to be related.

sections.heading: Design useful detections
body: Write the detection objective first: what behavior should be noticed, on which asset class, and what response should follow? Define the source data, grouping fields, time window, threshold, suppression, and known exceptions.
Test against synthetic positive and negative examples. Measure detection coverage and false positives; document blind spots and the expected human decision after an alert.

sections.heading: Triage consistently
body: Record what happened, when, which identity and assets are involved, what evidence supports the alert, and how confident the analyst is. Distinguish confirmed compromise from suspicious activity or a false positive.
Escalate using agreed severity and ownership. Preserve evidence, avoid unnecessary changes before coordination, and keep the incident lead informed of uncertainty and next actions.

assessment.q: Why should a detection rule include negative test cases?
opts: To make the dashboard look busier
To understand false positives and confirm the rule does not alert on expected activity
To remove the need for event sources
To guarantee that no incident will be missed
assessment.why: Negative cases show whether normal activity triggers the rule and help tune the detection.

assessment.q: A SIEM alert is raised for unusual sign-in activity. What should an analyst do before declaring an incident?
opts: Assume the alert is always correct
Correlate the event with identity, device, time, change, and business context
Delete the event to reduce noise
Notify everyone before validating the evidence
assessment.why: Triage combines multiple sources and checks confidence, impact, and context before escalation.

en.title: Incident response & digital forensics
overview: Use a repeatable lifecycle: prepare, detect, analyze, contain, eradicate, recover, and learn.

Build timelines from synthetic endpoint, identity, and application records.
Coordinate business owners, technical responders, legal/privacy contacts, and communications.

lessons.title: Evidence handling and preservation

lessons.title: Timeline reconstruction

lessons.outcome: Turn the incident into owned, measurable improvements.

lab.title: Run a tabletop incident with synthetic evidence
lab.brief: A fictional organization reports unusual account activity and a disrupted service. Use the supplied event bundle and role cards. This is a decision-making simulation; no real device is accessed.
steps: Assign the incident lead, technical responders, business owner, and communications contact.
Preserve the supplied event bundle and record its origin, version, receipt time, and handling history.
Build a timeline and label every entry as confirmed fact, interpretation, or open question.
Choose a proportionate containment option and explain operational impact and evidence-preservation trade-offs.
Define eradication, recovery, and post-recovery monitoring criteria with clear owners.
Write a post-incident review with root causes, contributing conditions, actions, owners, and due dates.

sections.heading: Prepare before the alert
body: Maintain an incident plan with roles, escalation paths, service owners, legal/privacy contacts, communications templates, and access to recovery resources. Exercise the plan so that responsibilities are understood before an event.
Define severity levels and decision authority. Prepare evidence locations, time synchronization, protected communication channels, and a method for recording important decisions.

sections.heading: Preserve evidence
body: Record where each item came from, who collected it, when, how it was handled, and where it is stored. Preserve original records and work from controlled copies when appropriate.
Restrict access to evidence and avoid collecting more personal or confidential data than necessary. Follow the organization’s retention, privacy, and legal requirements.

sections.heading: Contain with context
body: Containment options depend on the affected service, identity, and business impact. Coordinate with the incident lead and owner; consider reversibility, service continuity, and evidence preservation before a major change.
Keep a decision log with the reason, approver, time, expected effect, and validation result. Record what was not possible and why.

sections.heading: Recover and learn
body: Restore from a known-good state, verify identity and configuration, and monitor for recurrence before declaring full recovery. Service owners should confirm that business functions work as expected.
The post-incident review should identify root and contributing causes without blame, then assign measurable actions, owners, target dates, and a follow-up review.

assessment.q: During an incident, why preserve original evidence and record who handled it?
opts: It supports integrity, provenance, and later review
assessment.why: Evidence handling records help others understand where data came from and whether it may have changed.

assessment.q: During a suspected incident, which action best supports a defensible investigation?
opts: Change systems without recording the changes
Record decisions and timestamps, preserve relevant evidence, and follow the response plan
Share raw personal data in a public chat
Delete logs after writing a summary
assessment.why: Accurate records and controlled evidence handling help responders understand what happened and support later review.

overview: Use structured threat modeling to identify assets, trust boundaries, threat events, and mitigations.

lessons.outcome: Map interfaces and data flows that change the risk picture.

lessons.title: Attack-surface change review

lessons.title: Threat-informed improvement plan
lessons.outcome: Prioritize mitigations and define evidence that coverage improved.

lab.title: Threat-model a fictional member portal
lab.brief: Review a fictional service diagram, data classification, and business roles. Use threat categories to discuss design risks and defenses; do not attempt exploitation.
steps: List users, administrators, external services, sensitive data, and business-critical actions.
Draw trust boundaries and data flows for sign-in, profile updates, payments, and support.
For each boundary, brainstorm plausible threat events and the business effect.
Map each threat to preventive, detective, and recovery controls.
Review a sample threat-intelligence bulletin for source quality, age, relevance, and confidence.
Create a prioritized treatment plan and identify what telemetry would demonstrate improved coverage.

sections.heading: Model the system
body: Start with a system boundary, business purpose, users, administrators, data, external dependencies, and sensitive operations. Draw data flows and trust boundaries before brainstorming individual threats.
Use a consistent set of threat categories to prompt questions. The aim is not to predict every attack, but to uncover design assumptions and choose proportionate safeguards.

sections.heading: Evaluate intelligence carefully
body: Record the source, publication date, confidence, affected technology, relevance to your environment, and any handling restrictions. Intelligence can become stale or may not apply to a particular asset.
Corroborate important claims with authoritative vendor or internal evidence. Avoid copying indicators into production controls without an owner, test, and expiration/review plan.

sections.heading: Use behavior frameworks defensively
body: A public technique framework can provide a shared vocabulary for discussing observed behavior and defensive coverage. It is a classification aid, not proof that a specific event occurred.
For each relevant behavior, ask what telemetry could reveal it, what preventive control reduces the opportunity, and which response owner should be notified.

sections.heading: Prioritize mitigation
body: Rank model findings by business impact, plausibility, exposure, existing safeguards, and implementation cost. Record assumptions and uncertainty.
Revisit the model after major architecture, supplier, identity, or data-flow changes. A threat model is a living design artifact, not a one-time diagram.

assessment.q: What is the main purpose of a threat model?
opts: Predict every possible attack with certainty
Expose design assumptions and connect plausible threats to proportionate controls
assessment.why: Threat modeling is a structured way to reason about a system and improve its design; it is not a guarantee.

assessment.q: What is the main purpose of identifying trust boundaries during threat modeling?
opts: To list every tool in the environment
To identify where data or authority crosses between components and where controls are needed
To predict every future attack exactly
assessment.why: Trust boundaries highlight transitions between components, users, and privileges where assumptions and controls should be reviewed.

en.title: Governance, risk, compliance & privacy
overview: Translate business obligations into policies, standards, procedures, and measurable controls.
Understand risk acceptance, supplier assurance, evidence, audit, and exception management.
Map personal-data flows, purpose, retention, access, and deletion responsibilities.
Communicate compliance gaps without confusing a checklist with actual security.

lessons.title: Governance documents and ownership
lessons.outcome: Separate policy, standard, procedure, and evidence ownership.

lessons.title: Risk treatment and acceptance
lessons.outcome: Document reduce, avoid, transfer, or accept decisions and approvals.

lessons.title: Privacy and data lifecycle

lessons.title: Supplier and third-party assurance
lessons.outcome: Review data access, responsibilities, incident notice, and exit terms.

lessons.title: Audit evidence and control testing

lab.title: Build a risk, privacy, and control register
lab.brief: Use a fictional service with synthetic customer data, supplier dependencies, and policy requirements. The exercise is a documentation and decision workshop, not legal advice.
steps: List the applicable business commitments and map each to an internal policy or operational control.
Map the sample personal-data lifecycle: collection, purpose, access, sharing, retention, and deletion.
Create a risk register with owner, impact, likelihood, treatment, evidence, and review date.
Review the supplier card for data access, subcontracting, security contact, incident notice, and exit provisions.
Select evidence for three controls and explain whether it demonstrates design, operation, or both.
Write an exception record with justification, compensating measure, approver, expiry, and reassessment trigger.

guide.title: Governance, risk, compliance, and privacy guide

sections.heading: Turn obligations into controls
body: Policies state intent and responsibilities; standards define required outcomes; procedures explain repeatable work; evidence shows that the control is operating. Assign an owner and review date to each important document.
Map requirements to controls and evidence. Avoid claiming compliance because a policy exists; test whether the control is implemented, used, and reviewed.

sections.heading: Treat risk transparently
body: Risk treatment options include reducing, avoiding, transferring, or accepting risk. Acceptance should be explicit, approved by the right authority, time-bound where appropriate, and supported by an explanation.
Maintain risk owners, actions, target dates, residual risk, and review triggers. Escalate overdue high-impact actions rather than silently extending them.

sections.heading: Respect privacy and data lifecycle
body: For each personal-data set, record purpose, source, legal/business basis as applicable, access roles, recipients, location, retention, deletion, and safeguards. Collect only what the service needs.
Privacy requirements depend on jurisdiction and context. Involve the appropriate privacy or legal specialist for real deployments; a course worksheet is not a legal determination.

sections.heading: Assess suppliers and evidence
body: Understand which supplier can access what data, where it is processed, how incidents are reported, what assurance is available, and how the relationship can end.
Good evidence demonstrates an operating control: a sample review, approved change, system setting, or tested restoration. Keep evidence relevant, dated, attributable, and protected.

assessment.q: A policy document exists, but there is no evidence that staff follow it. What can the organization safely claim?
opts: The policy exists, but operating effectiveness has not been demonstrated
assessment.why: A document proves that a policy exists, not that a control is implemented or effective.

assessment.q: A service collects personal data that is no longer needed for its stated purpose. Which principle should guide the review?
opts: Keep all data forever in case it is useful
Define purpose, limit collection, retention, access, and deletion according to applicable requirements
assessment.why: Privacy governance requires clear purposes and controlled data lifecycle decisions, including retention and deletion.

Understand where simple automation helps and where human approval is required.
Write concise findings, runbooks, and status updates for technical and non-technical readers.
Prepare a portfolio that demonstrates reasoning, documentation, and responsible practice.

lessons.outcome: Create a ticket with scope, owner, evidence, priority, and next action.

lessons.title: Automation boundaries and approvals

lab.title: Turn a synthetic alert into a complete security work item
lab.brief: Use a fictional alert and its evidence to create a ticket, runbook excerpt, escalation note, and management summary. No real notification or system integration is involved.
steps: Write a ticket with concise title, scope, asset, priority, evidence, confidence, and owner.
Separate actions that can be automated safely from actions that require human authorization.
Draft a runbook with preconditions, decision points, expected results, and rollback guidance.
Select two operational metrics and define how they could be distorted or misread.
Prepare a technical handover and a non-technical summary from the same evidence.
Add the exercise to a portfolio with synthetic-data notice, learning reflection, and limitations.

sections.heading: Make work traceable
body: A useful ticket records the affected asset, owner, scope, priority, evidence, confidence, current status, and next action. Use consistent states so work can be handed over without losing context.
Link related changes, incidents, and risks. Record approvals and decisions in the system of record rather than relying on informal chat alone.

sections.heading: Automate with guardrails
body: Automation is best for repeatable, low-risk, observable tasks such as enrichment, formatting, routing, and reminder workflows. Define permissions, logs, failure handling, and a way to stop it.
Require human approval for actions that could interrupt services, change privileged access, delete evidence, or affect many users. Test automation with synthetic data before operational use.

sections.heading: Write useful runbooks
body: A runbook should state purpose, scope, prerequisites, roles, decision points, expected outputs, escalation, rollback, and evidence to retain. Keep each action small enough to verify.
Review runbooks after exercises and incidents. Remove outdated references, name an owner, and test that another qualified person can follow the procedure.

sections.heading: Communicate with precision
body: Lead with impact and decision needed. Present the evidence, confidence, uncertainty, options, owner, and next update. Avoid alarmist language and unsupported certainty.

For a portfolio, explain the problem, your authorized scope, your reasoning, the artifacts you created, what you learned, and what you did not test. Never publish real credentials or third-party sensitive data.

assessment.q: Which task is most appropriate for low-risk automation without per-event human approval?
opts: Changing administrator access for all users
Formatting and routing a security ticket using defined rules
assessment.why: Low-risk, reversible, observable administrative tasks are better candidates; high-impact actions need approval.

assessment.q: A repetitive security task is being automated. What must be defined before the automation is used operationally?
opts: An accountable owner, approved scope, logging, failure handling, and a way to reverse or stop the action
A promise that automation cannot fail
assessment.why: Operational automation needs ownership, boundaries, auditability, safe failure behavior, and human approval where impact is high.

lab.title: Integrated assessment of the fictional Northstar service
lab.brief: This final exercise combines a fictional architecture, asset register, access matrix, code-review excerpts, cloud configuration, synthetic event logs, and an incident timeline. All evidence is course-created. The goal is a professional defensive assessment, not to compromise a system.
steps: Read the scope, business objectives, data classifications, and allowed evidence sources. Record assumptions and missing evidence.
Build an asset and trust-boundary map; identify critical services, identities, suppliers, and data stores.
Review the access matrix, application notes, and cloud configuration. Write findings with evidence, impact, confidence, and remediation.
Analyze synthetic telemetry and build a timeline. Recommend proportionate response, evidence preservation, and recovery validation.
Create a risk-ranked remediation roadmap with owners, target dates, dependencies, and temporary controls.
Deliver an executive summary, technical report, incident note, and 10-minute presentation outline.
evidence: Prioritized technical findings and treatment plan
Executive and technical report with presentation outline

sections.heading: Start with scope and evidence
body: Read the business brief before reviewing technical details. Record what is in scope, which activities are allowed, who owns the service, and which evidence sources are provided.
Maintain an evidence register with identifier, source, date, handling notes, relevance, and limitation. Mark statements as fact, interpretation, or assumption.

sections.heading: Connect findings across domains
body: A strong assessment connects identity, endpoint, network, application, cloud, and monitoring controls. Avoid writing isolated observations that do not explain the business consequence.
For each finding, record affected asset, condition, evidence, impact, confidence, owner, recommendation, and a safe validation method. Do not overstate what synthetic evidence proves.

sections.heading: Prioritize and plan remediation
body: Group related findings into themes such as identity governance, exposed services, insecure data handling, insufficient telemetry, or recovery readiness. Prioritize based on impact, exposure, confidence, and implementation dependencies.
Give every action an owner, target date, acceptance criterion, and evidence of closure. Track temporary mitigations and accepted risks separately from completed remediation.

sections.heading: Present and defend the result
body: The executive summary should lead with business impact, top decisions, and residual risk. The technical report should contain enough evidence for a qualified reader to understand and retest the issue.
Include scope, methods, limitations, assumptions, and items not assessed. A professional conclusion is clear about what is known, what remains uncertain, and what should happen next.

assessment.q: Which report statement is the most defensible when a data source was unavailable during the exercise?
opts: The relevant control could not be assessed from the supplied evidence; follow-up evidence is required
The missing source proves an incident
assessment.why: A professional report states evidence limitations and avoids making unsupported positive or negative claims.

assessment.q: A capstone report contains an observation from a data source that was incomplete. How should the finding be written?
opts: State it as a confirmed compromise
Describe the evidence, confidence, limitation, potential impact, and follow-up needed
Claim the entire service is secure
assessment.why: Professional reporting distinguishes facts, interpretation, assumptions, and missing evidence. It should not overstate what the source proves.

sections.heading: Начинайте с активов и последствий
body: Сначала выясните, что организация защищает и почему это важно. Активом может быть информация, сервис, устройство, учётная запись, связь с поставщиком или способность продолжать работу. Назначьте владельца, который отвечает за решения.

Описывайте ущерб понятными деловыми словами: остановка сервиса, изменение записей, раскрытие персональных данных, финансовые потери, риски для людей или потеря доверия. Не путайте само оповещение инструмента с риском.

sections.heading: Используйте единую модель риска
body: Полезное описание риска связывает угрозу, слабое место или экспозицию, актив и вероятное последствие. Зафиксируйте вероятность, ущерб, существующие меры, неопределённость и ответственного за обработку риска.

Оценки риска помогают расставлять приоритеты, но не являются точными научными измерениями. Используйте простую шкалу, определите её и поясните причины оценки. Пересматривайте её при изменении среды или появлении новых доказательств.

sections.heading: Выбирайте эшелонированные меры
body: Превентивные меры снижают вероятность события; детективные помогают его заметить; меры реагирования ограничивают последствия; меры восстановления возвращают сервис в надёжное состояние. Одна мера редко закрывает все сценарии отказа.

Отдавайте предпочтение проверяемым мерам. Политики резервного копирования недостаточно: восстановление нужно тестировать. Политики безопасности недостаточно: нужны ответственные, обучение и понятный порядок исключений.

sections.heading: Работайте профессионально
body: Письменное разрешение должно определять владельца, разрешённые активы и действия, период, правила работы с данными, контакты и условия остановки. Если границы неясны или среда отличается от описания, остановитесь и обратитесь к владельцу.

Собирайте минимум необходимых доказательств, защищайте их, записывайте способ получения и передавайте только уполномоченным адресатам. Указывайте ограничения и неопределённость, не выдавая предположения за факты.

assessment.q: Сервис доступен, но записи в нём изменили без разрешения. Какое свойство безопасности прежде всего нарушено?
assessment.why: Целостность отвечает за точность информации и изменение данных только в рамках разрешённых процессов.

assessment.q: В задании на оценку не указано, какие системы входят в границы работ. Как поступить профессионально?
opts: Проверять только те системы, которые интересны
Остановиться и получить письменное подтверждение границ от владельца
assessment.why: Письменное разрешение и чёткие границы — обязательные условия. Добрые намерения не заменяют разрешение.

guide.title: Руководство по защите Linux и конечных устройств

sections.heading: Изучите устройство до изменений
body: Зафиксируйте редакцию ОС, уровень обновлений, роль устройства, владельца, установленные службы и обрабатываемые данные. Неподдерживаемая система — это риск жизненного цикла, а не просто напоминание об обновлении.
Определите, какие службы нужны для рабочих задач. Безопасная базовая конфигурация начинается с понятного назначения устройства и устранения ненужной экспозиции без нарушения рабочих процессов.

sections.heading: Применяйте наименьшие привилегии
body: Используйте именные учётные записи и группы, соответствующие реальным обязанностям. Отделяйте повседневную работу от администрирования, а сервисным учётным записям давайте только нужные процессу права.

Для каждого файла или каталога проверяйте владельца, группу и требования к доступу. Не используйте широкие права записи как быстрое исправление. У исключений должны быть причина, владелец и дата пересмотра.

sections.heading: Защищайте и наблюдайте конечные устройства
body: Обновляйте поддерживаемые ОС и приложения по контролируемому процессу. Используйте шифрование диска, автоматическую блокировку экрана, политику локального межсетевого экрана и защиту конечных устройств в соответствии с ролью устройства.
Собирайте полезные события безопасности, ограничивая чувствительные данные в журналах. Проверяйте синхронизацию времени и доставку важных событий в центральную систему мониторинга.

sections.heading: Безопасно вносите изменения
body: Используйте запись об изменении: цель, границы, владелец, риск, планируемое действие, тест, откат и результат. Меняйте по одному элементу, чтобы понимать причину неожиданного эффекта.
После изменения проверяйте и безопасность, и удобство работы. Убедитесь, что сотрудники выполняют утверждённые задачи, журналы формируются, а устройство можно восстановить.

assessment.q: Команда предлагает дать всем локальным пользователям право записи в общий каталог приложения, чтобы исправить ошибку прав. Как поступить лучше?
opts: Применить, потому что приложению нужно записывать файлы
Определить конкретный процесс и путь, затем выдать минимально необходимые права
assessment.why: Наименьшие привилегии означают, что только конкретная служба получает доступ, необходимый для определённой операции.

assessment.q: На рабочей станции отсутствуют несколько обновлений безопасности. Какие доказательства лучше всего подтверждают завершение исправления?
opts: Актуальный инвентарь патчей и успешная запись проверки/перезагрузки
Запись о том, что устройством редко пользуются
assessment.why: Результат нужно проверить в системном инвентаре: подтвердить уровень обновлений и необходимость перезагрузки.

guide.title: Руководство по сетевой безопасности и интерпретации трафика

sections.heading: Прослеживайте весь путь
body: Запрос пользователя может включать локальный DNS, рекурсивный резолвер, маршрутизацию, транспортное соединение, согласование TLS, прокси и сервис приложения. Записывайте каждый этап, а не только имя узла.
По утверждённой схеме и инвентарю определяйте ожидаемые источник, назначение, цель и владельца. Один порт или протокол не доказывает, что служба безопасна или небезопасна.

sections.heading: Осторожно интерпретируйте доказательства
body: Сводка пакетов может показывать время, конечные точки, метаданные протокола и часть незашифрованного содержимого. TLS обычно защищает полезную нагрузку приложения, но некоторые метаданные соединения остаются видимыми наблюдателям на маршруте.
Отсутствие события может означать, что сбор данных был недоступен, задержан, отфильтрован или неполон. Перед выводами укажите источник данных и границы наблюдения.

sections.heading: Проектируйте сетевые границы
body: Разделяйте устройства пользователей, административный доступ, публичные сервисы, компоненты приложений и хранилища чувствительных данных по их назначению. Разрешайте только документированные потоки с владельцем и обоснованием.
Пересматривайте правила после изменений и по расписанию. Удаляйте устаревшие исключения, журналируйте важные разрешённые и запрещённые события и проверяйте легитимные потоки сервисов.

sections.heading: Делайте рекомендации применимыми
body: Для каждой рекомендации укажите затронутую зону, владельца, бизнес-цель, ожидаемую пользу, операционное влияние и способ проверки. Предпочитайте небольшие проверяемые изменения с возможностью отката.
Не делайте вывод о компрометации по одному незнакомому адресу. Сопоставляйте сетевые наблюдения с данными конечных устройств, идентификации, приложений и изменениями.

assessment.q: В сводке пакетов видно TLS-соединение с сервисом. Какой вывод можно сделать только на основании этого факта?

assessment.q: Сетевое правило разрешает всем пользовательским сегментам подключаться к чувствительной базе данных. Какое улучшение лучше сделать первым?
opts: Ограничить доступ конкретным потоком приложения и утверждёнными ролями
